title: Design a Ride-Sharing Service (Uber / Lyft)
tagline: Match a rider to the best nearby driver in seconds, track everyone in real time, and never double-book a car.
summary: Geo-matching, real-time location, dispatch, surge, exactly-once trips.

paragraphs: Ride-sharing combines two hard sub-problems: a geospatial 'find nearby drivers' search (the proximity-service problem) and a real-time matching/dispatch engine that pairs one rider with one driver under heavy contention. Scope which you'll focus on — usually matching is the headline.

blocks.title: Functional
items: Riders request a ride from A to B; the system finds and assigns a nearby driver.
Drivers broadcast their location continuously and accept/decline requests.
Both sides see each other's live location and ETA during the trip.
Fare calculation, trip lifecycle (requested → matched → in-progress → completed).

blocks.title: Non-functional
items: Low latency on matching — riders abandon if it takes more than a few seconds.
High availability — an outage means lost rides and revenue, and stranded users.
Location updates at massive write volume (millions of drivers pinging every few seconds).
Consistency where it counts: a driver must never be assigned to two riders at once.

blocks.text: Two insights to lead with: (1) driver location is high-frequency, ephemeral, write-heavy data → keep it in an in-memory geo-index, not a disk DB; (2) assigning a driver to a rider is a contention/consistency problem → it needs a lock or a single-threaded-per-driver decision so two riders can't grab the same car.

items.detail: Say 1M active drivers each sending a location every 4s → 1M / 4 = 250,000 location writes/sec. This dominates write load and rules out a disk-based store for live locations.
Far lower — maybe ~10k–50k requests/sec at peak. The expensive part of each is the geo-search + matching, not raw volume.
Completed trips are durable records (a few KB each) → a relational/wide-column store; tens of millions of trips/day. Live locations are ephemeral and stay in memory.

blocks.caption: Separate the high-write location pipeline from the trip/matching path. WebSockets keep both sides live.

items.title: Drivers stream location
items.detail: Driver apps send GPS pings over a persistent connection. The Location Service updates the driver's cell in an in-memory geospatial index (Redis geo / quadtree) keyed by geohash. Old positions are overwritten — only the current location matters.

items.title: Rider requests a ride
items.detail: The Matching Service computes the rider's geohash cell, queries the in-memory index for available drivers in that cell + neighboring cells, and ranks candidates by ETA (real road distance, not straight-line).

items.title: Dispatch & lock
items.detail: It offers the ride to the best driver and locks that driver (status = 'offered') so no other match can grab them. If the driver declines or times out, release the lock and offer the next candidate.

items.title: Trip lifecycle
items.detail: On acceptance, create a durable trip record (matched). Both apps get live updates via WebSocket. On completion, compute fare and persist the trip.

sections.title: 4. The matching & dispatch engine (the hard part)

paragraphs: Matching is where the design earns its keep. The core challenge: many riders and drivers in the same hot area, and you must assign each driver to exactly one rider with low latency and no double-booking.

items.detail: Two riders' searches can return the same driver simultaneously. Serialize the assignment: either use a distributed lock on the driver id (e.g., Redis SET NX with a TTL), or route all decisions for a driver/region through a single owner (consistent-hash drivers to matching workers) so one worker decides per driver. The TTL ensures a crashed worker doesn't lock a driver forever.
The closest driver as the crow flies may be across a river. Rank candidates by predicted time-to-pickup using a routing/ETA service that accounts for roads and traffic.
Lock the chosen driver, offer the trip, and wait a few seconds. On decline/timeout, release and try the next candidate. This sequential offer protocol keeps assignment atomic.

Instead of greedily matching each request as it arrives, collect requests over a short window and solve a global assignment (bipartite matching) to minimize total wait — better outcomes in dense areas at the cost of a small delay.

blocks.title: The hot-cell problem
blocks.text: During a concert or rush hour, one geohash cell gets a flood of both location pings and ride requests. Mitigate with finer-grained cells in dense areas (or an adaptive quadtree), shard the matching workers by region, and replicate the in-memory index. Be ready to discuss this — it's the classic follow-up.

items.detail: During a trip, the driver's pings are pushed to the rider over a WebSocket (and vice-versa) so the map updates in real time. This rides on the same location pipeline, filtered to the trip's participants.

A background job continuously computes the supply/demand ratio per region (available drivers vs open requests) and sets a surge multiplier. This is naturally eventually consistent and computed from the same location/request streams.

The trip lifecycle (requested → matched → ongoing → completed) must be strongly consistent and idempotent — a retried 'accept' must not create two trips. Use an idempotency key on trip creation and a state machine with valid transitions.
On completion, charge via the payment system asynchronously (queue the fare event); apply idempotency so a retry never double-charges. (See the payment-system case study.)

blocks.text: Frame the whole system as two decoupled pipelines: a write-heavy, eventually-consistent location/geo pipeline (in-memory, sharded by region), and a strongly-consistent, idempotent trip/matching pipeline that locks drivers to avoid double-booking. Knowing which half needs which consistency model is the senior signal.

cheatsheet: Two sub-problems: geospatial 'find nearby drivers' (proximity) + real-time matching/dispatch under contention.
Driver locations are high-frequency, ephemeral, write-heavy (~250k pings/sec) → in-memory geo-index (Redis geo / quadtree), not a disk DB.
Match: geohash the rider, query the cell + neighbors, rank candidates by ETA (road/traffic), not straight-line distance.
Prevent double-assignment: distributed lock on driver id (Redis SET NX + TTL) or consistent-hash drivers to one matching worker.
Offer → accept → fallback (sequential), or batch matching over a short window for globally better assignments.
Hot-cell problem (events/rush hour): finer cells, shard matching by region, replicate the index.
Trip lifecycle is a strongly-consistent, idempotent state machine; live tracking + surge ride on the location streams (eventually consistent).

questions.prompt: Two riders request a ride at the same instant and your geo-search returns the same nearby driver for both. How do you guarantee that driver is assigned to only one of them?
questions.hint: Serialize the assignment decision per driver.
answer: This is a classic race: two independent matching computations both see the same available driver and could both assign it. The fix is to serialize the *assignment decision* for any given driver so only one can win. Two clean approaches: (1) a distributed lock keyed on the driver id — before offering, do an atomic `SET driver:{id}:lock = tripId NX EX <ttl>` in Redis; only the request that successfully sets it may offer the ride, the other sees the key exists and moves to its next candidate. The TTL is essential so a matching worker that crashes mid-offer doesn't lock the driver forever. (2) Consistent-hash drivers to matching workers so every decision about a given driver is owned by exactly one worker/thread, which then makes assignments sequentially with no cross-worker race.

Either way, once a driver is locked we mark them 'offered/assigned' so subsequent geo-searches exclude them. If the driver declines or the offer times out, we release the lock (or it expires) and the driver becomes available again. The driver's status transitions through a small state machine (available → offered → on-trip → available), and trip creation uses an idempotency key so even a retried 'accept' can't spawn two trips. The key principle: geo-search can be eventually consistent and parallel, but the assignment must funnel through a single serialized decision per driver.
keyPoints: Serialize assignment per driver — geo-search alone isn't enough
Distributed lock (Redis SET NX + TTL) or consistent-hash driver→one worker
TTL/expiry so a crashed worker doesn't lock a driver forever
Driver state machine + idempotent trip creation; exclude locked drivers from searches
followUps: A driver declines after being offered — how do you fall back quickly without re-running the whole search from scratch?

questions.prompt: 1M drivers each send a location update every 4 seconds. Where do you store these and why not a traditional database?
questions.hint: ~250k writes/sec of ephemeral data where only the latest value matters.
answer: That's ~250,000 writes/sec, and crucially the data is ephemeral — only a driver's *current* location matters, not the history of every ping. Writing 250k rows/sec to a disk-backed relational database would be a brutal, pointless write storm: you'd be paying durability and indexing costs for data you overwrite seconds later, and disk-based geo queries would add latency to the matching hot path.

Instead, keep live locations in an in-memory geospatial index — Redis with its geo commands, or an in-memory quadtree/grid keyed by geohash. Each ping updates the driver's position in place (overwriting the old one), which is a cheap memory operation, and 'find drivers near this cell' is a fast in-memory lookup. We only periodically checkpoint to durable storage for crash recovery, and we persist *completed trips* (which are durable, valuable records) to a proper database. This split — ephemeral high-write location data in memory, durable trip records on disk — is exactly the regime distinction from the proximity-service problem: tailor the store to whether the data is transient and write-heavy or durable and queryable.
keyPoints: ~250k writes/sec of ephemeral 'latest location only' data
Disk DB = wasteful write storm + slow geo queries on the hot path
In-memory geo-index (Redis geo / quadtree), update in place; periodic checkpoint
Persist completed trips to a durable DB; split ephemeral vs durable storage
followUps: How would you handle a hot cell (a stadium emptying out) flooding both pings and ride requests?
